name: Maldives
summary: About 1,200 coral islands in the Indian Ocean; a Muslim sultanate for centuries, a British protectorate until 1965, a republic since 1968; the lowest-lying country in the world.

knownFor.label: Cowrie shells
knownFor.note: Exported as money across Asia and Africa.

location.value: Indian Ocean; about 298 km² of land spread over roughly 90,000 km² of sea.

terrain.value: Flat coral islands, mostly under 1.5 m above sea level.

climate.value: Hot and humid tropical climate all year, with a wet south-west monsoon (about May–November) and a drier north-east monsoon.

resources.value: Tuna and other fish, coral reefs and white beaches that attract tourists, and coconut palms; almost no land for farming.

disasters.value: The tsunami of 26 December 2004 caused damage of over US$400 million (about 62% of GDP); 102 Maldivians and 6 foreigners died and six islands were destroyed.

population.value: 601,269 in a 2024 estimate; the 2022 census counted 515,132, including 132,493 foreigners.

urbanisation.value: About a third live on Malé, one of the densest cities.

disease.value: Good basic health care; rising diabetes.

migration.value: Many people move from outer atolls to Malé, and tens of thousands of workers come from Bangladesh, India and other countries.

economicBase.value: Tourism is 28% of GDP and over 60% of foreign-exchange receipts; fishing is the second-largest sector.

tradeRoutes.value: Velana International Airport near Malé and shipping through Malé port; it lies close to major Indian Ocean shipping lanes.

wealth.value: An upper-middle-income country, among the richest per person in South Asia, though heavily in debt.

moneyAndTax.value: The Maldivian rufiyaa (100 laari), issued by the Maldives Monetary Authority; tourism taxes are a major source of revenue.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic with a unicameral People’s Majlis; independence from the UK on 26 July 1965 and a republic from 11 November 1968.

keyRulers.value: The Maldives’ presidents since the 1968 republic are not named here.

succession.value: The sultanate ended in 1968; presidents were confirmed by referendum until the first multi-party presidential election in 2008.

institutions.value: The People’s Majlis (parliament), the Supreme Court (created in 2008) and independent commissions such as the elections commission.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between Gayoom and Nasheed camps.

armyAndTech.value: The Maldives National Defence Force, including a coast guard; India helped defeat a mercenary coup attempt in 1988.

majorWars.value: No wars since independence; the main security crisis was the 1988 coup attempt by foreign mercenaries.

territoryChange.value: No changes since independence; a breakaway republic in the southern atolls (1959–63) had ended shortly before.

alliancesRivals.value: Balances ties with India and China; a founding member of SAARC (1985); left the Commonwealth in 2016 and rejoined in 2020.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state; it is known for its global campaigning on climate change.

scienceEducation.value: High literacy and free schooling; the Maldives National University (2011) and the Islamic University of Maldives.

openness.value: Opened to international tourism in 1972, when the first resort was built; very open to tourists but strict about religion.

communicationTransport.value: Boats (dhonis and speedboats), seaplanes and domestic flights link the atolls; a bridge has joined Malé to the airport island since 2018.

religion.value: Sunni Islam is the official religion and citizens must follow it; the last Buddhist king, Dhovemi, converted in 1153 according to the page, which also cites 1193.

languageWriting.value: Dhivehi, an Indo-Aryan language related to Sinhala, written right to left in the Thaana script; English is widely used.

artsArchitecture.value: The Old Friday Mosque in Malé (1658), with carved coral stone, lacquer work, and bodu beru drumming.

socialStructure.value: Mostly Maldivian Muslims sharing one language, with a richer Malé elite and a large group of foreign workers.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong shared identity based on Islam, the Dhivehi language and island life on the atolls.

dailyLife.value: Meals of tuna, rice, coconut and roshi flatbread, such as mas huni for breakfast; many work in resorts or fishing.

neighbours.value: India and its Lakshadweep islands to the north, Sri Lanka to the north-east, and the Chagos islands to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Sunni Islam shapes law and daily life; since the 2000s, concern about climate change and democratic reform have been key ideas.

colonisation.value: The Portuguese set up a garrison in 1558; the Dutch gained influence from the mid-17th century; Britain made it a protectorate in 1887.

riseSignals.value: Buddhism probably spread to the Maldives in the 3rd century BCE; the last Buddhist king, Dhovemi, converted to Islam in 1153 (or 1193).

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; the tourism boom since the 1970s brought the greatest prosperity in its history.

declineSignals.value: Rising seas threaten the low islands; some expect many to become uninhabitable, while others say reclamation and coral growth can adapt.

outcome.value: An agreement of 26 July 1965 ended British control of defence and foreign affairs; the republic was declared on 11 November 1968, ending the monarchy.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
